title: What Needle Size to Use for 11, 14, 16 and 18 Count Aida

seo.title: What Needle Size to Use for 11, 14, 16 and 18 Count Aida
seo.meta_description: Practical needle-size guide for 11, 14, 16 and 18 count Aida, including sizes 22, 24, 26 and 28 and signs that a needle is too large or small.
seo.search_intent: Stitchers who want to know which tapestry needle size to use for 11, 14, 16 or 18 count Aida.

excerpt: Aida count gives you a useful needle-size starting point, but the best needle passes easily without enlarging holes or damaging floss.
content_html:
Cross stitch is normally worked with a blunt tapestry needle. Needle numbering runs in the opposite direction from physical size: a size 22 needle is larger than a size 28. Lower-count Aida has larger holes and generally suits a larger needle, while finer fabric counts work comfortably with smaller needles.

As a practical starting point, 11-count Aida often pairs with size 22, 14-count with size 24, 16-count with size 26, and 18-count with size 26 or 28. These are useful conventions rather than strict rules. Strand count, fabric stiffness, personal grip and comfort can change the best choice.

11-count Aida: size 22 is a strong starting point

11-count Aida has large visible blocks and relatively open holes. A size 22 needle has enough body and a generous eye for the larger strand counts often used on this fabric.

If you stitch with three strands of floss, a much finer needle can make threading awkward and increase friction as the thicker bundle passes through the eye.

If size 22 visibly enlarges the holes or leaves the fabric distorted, try one size finer. The cloth should settle back into shape instead of showing a permanent opening at every stitch.

14-count Aida: size 24 is the classic default

14-count Aida is one of the most common fabrics and is often worked with two strands. A size 24 tapestry needle offers an eye that is easy to thread while still passing comfortably through the holes.

Many stitchers also use size 26 when they prefer a finer needle. That is perfectly workable as long as the eye does not abrade the floss and the needle remains comfortable to handle.

For beginners, size 24 is often easier to thread. After a few projects, comparing it with a 26 is a simple way to discover your preference.

16-count Aida: size 26 usually feels well proportioned

The holes on 16-count Aida are smaller, and a size 26 usually moves through them with less resistance than a 24. With two strands of cotton, the eye is still practical without opening the fabric unnecessarily.

A slightly larger needle can work on softer 16-count cloth, but you should not need to push hard or force the eye through the hole.

Watch the floss as well. If it begins to fuzz near the eye or feels heavily rubbed during every pass, the eye may be too tight for the number of strands you are using.

18-count Aida: compare size 26 and 28

On 18-count Aida, many stitchers prefer size 28 because the smaller needle suits the finer holes. Others use size 26, particularly with two strands when a slightly larger eye is more convenient.

With one strand, a size 28 often feels naturally proportioned. With two strands, try both sizes for a few stitches before committing to the entire project.

The correct needle is not necessarily the smallest one that can physically pass through the fabric. If threading is frustrating, the needle bends too easily in your grip, or the floss wears quickly, size 26 may be the better tool.

Signs that a needle is too large

An oversized needle can require more pressure, enlarge the holes or separate the fabric fibers more than necessary. It may also feel clumsy when you return through areas that already contain several stitches.

On the back, very open holes can make thread endings feel less secure. On the front, dense areas may show a more distorted grid.

The needle should slide with only light resistance. A small amount of contact is normal, but you should not feel as though you are piercing a tightly woven fabric.

Signs that a needle is too small

A very fine needle may have an eye that is inconvenient for two or three strands. It can also be uncomfortable to hold if you have larger hands or stitch for long sessions.

If floss separates, frays near the eye, or every color change becomes difficult to thread, move up one needle size.

The most useful test is to keep two neighboring sizes available and stitch ten or twenty crosses with each. You will quickly notice which one passes more smoothly, protects the floss better and feels more comfortable.

A simple reference is size 22 for 11-count, 24 for 14-count, 26 for 16-count, and 26–28 for 18-count. From there, adjust for strand count, fabric and your own hand. A good needle should work with the cloth rather than forcing it.
